**Authors:** Dora Gicheva, Julie A. Edmunds, Bryan C. Hutchins, Nir Eilam, and Nina Arshavsky
**Review Date:** 2026-09-02
**Model:** Claude (via Claude Code)
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader's Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Gicheva, Edmunds, Hutchins, Eilam, and Arshavsky (2026) is the best-scoped US descriptive evidence to date on how first-year college performance moved across the pandemic: near-universe linked K-12-to-college records for North Carolina's public four-year and community college systems (about 403,000 immediate enrollees from the high school classes of 2015–2022), identical outcome definitions in both sectors, and a horizon that reaches the 2022–23 academic year — well past the Spring-2020 window that bounds most prior work. Several facts it documents are robust and worth citing. The Spring 2020 jump in four-year completion (about +5 pp, +0.75 earned credits) was a grading-policy artifact, with pass-type grades rising from roughly 1.5% to over 11% of courses; community colleges show the mirror image, an 11 pp withdrawal spike offset by 9 pp fewer D/F grades, replicating Bulman and Fairlie's California finding in a second state. The deepest four-year declines arrived with the 2021 cohort (about −0.5 to −0.6 earned credits and −2 to −3 pp completion in 2021–22), not during the acute disruption, and aggregate completion was back near baseline by 2022–23. Fall-to-spring persistence fell 1.5–2 pp at four-year institutions (against a 95% baseline) and about 3.5 pp at community colleges for the 2020–21 cohorts. And relative gaps in successful completion widened for below-median-GPA students (the largest and clearest subgroup result, roughly 5–9 pp at four-year institutions) and by 2–4 pp for underrepresented-minority, economically disadvantaged, and female students. The paper's most quotable claim, however — that these declines "have persisted" and outcomes "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for those groups — is a claim about levels that no exhibit supports: Figure 4 plots only subgroup-minus-reference-group differences, the reference-group trajectories are never shown, and the aggregate series sit near zero at the last observation. All five sub-reviews converge on this point independently. Three further calibrations matter. The community-college decline is confounded with the RISE developmental-education reform (2019–2021), which moved weaker students into exactly the credit-bearing courses the analysis retains, and the last Spring 2023 community-college points are at or above baseline despite the text's "sustained" language. Spring-semester estimates condition on falling fall-to-spring persistence, so the visible fall/spring sawtooth and any "recovery" read off the right edge of the figures are partly survivorship. And inference for the four-year results rests on 16 clusters with no small-sample correction, while not one coefficient is reported numerically and there is no data-availability statement or code. The authors are candid that the design is descriptive — no untreated group, no separation from concurrent shocks — and that candor is the right frame. Cite the paper for the timing of the decline, the sector-mechanism contrast, and the widening relative gap by prior achievement; attach caveats to every "persistent decline" phrasing, to the female result, and to the community-college story as a pandemic effect; and obtain the Online Appendix (and ideally the coefficient tables from the authors) before building on specific magnitudes.

#### Key Strengths

- A rare data asset used at the right scale: course-level transcripts for the near-universe of North Carolina public high school graduates enrolling immediately in the 16-campus UNC System or the 58-college NCCCS (210,008 and 192,793 students), linked to NCDPI K-12 records for baseline GPA, economic disadvantage, English learner, and disability status — no survey nonresponse, both sectors on identical outcome definitions.
- A horizon no earlier US study could offer: extending through the class of 2022 lets the paper show that the deepest four-year declines came with the 2021 cohort, after the acute disruption, and that aggregate completion had returned near baseline by 2022–23 — the paper's most defensible novel finding.
- Outcome decomposition that reveals mechanism, not just magnitude: reporting attempted credits, earned credits, C-or-better share, and withdrawal/incomplete share side by side shows that four-year declines ran through D/F grades with flat withdrawals while community-college declines ran through withdrawals and rising part-time enrollment, and it diagnoses the Spring 2020 spikes as grading-policy incidence using footnote 4's pass-grade shares.
- Unusual candor about design limits and measurement threats: the Conclusion states plainly that the study is descriptive and cannot disentangle the pandemic from concurrent shocks; the text warns explicitly that a negative Figure 4 coefficient need not mean a subgroup declined; and the GPA scale/weighting changes, RISE, and the pass-grade surge are all disclosed.
- Numerical fidelity inside the Results: the magnitudes the prose states (0.75 credits, 5 pp, 11 pp, 9 pp, 1–2 pp persistence) verify against the figures, so the body text can be trusted where it sits next to its exhibit.

#### Key Concerns

- The headline subgroup claim is a level claim resting on relative coefficients: the abstract and introduction say declines "have persisted" and outcomes "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for URE, economically disadvantaged, low-GPA, and female students, but Figure 4 shows only differences from the reference group's change, the reference-group coefficients are never reported, and the aggregate series are near baseline at the end — the paper commits, in its most-read paragraphs, the exact inference error it warns against on page 10.
- The community-college story is confounded with RISE and overstated at the endpoint: the developmental-education exclusion interacts with a 2019–2021 reform that pushed weaker students into the retained credit-bearing courses, the main text offers no specification that holds course mix fixed, and the text's "sustained increase in course withdrawals" is contradicted by Figure 2c/2d's final Spring 2023 points at or above baseline.
- Sample selection and spring survivorship are unaddressed: enrollment fell differentially on exactly the margins studied (footnote 3), spring outcomes condition on fall-to-spring persistence that itself fell 1.5–3.5 pp, producing a visible fall/spring sawtooth; and because each cohort contributes one first year, "rebounded" means a later cohort did better, not that any affected student recovered.
- Inference and verification are thin: 16 four-year clusters with no small-sample correction, no pre-trend tests despite visibly sloped pre-periods in Figures 2a, 2b, 3b, and 3d, no multiplicity adjustment across roughly 200 reported coefficients, no coefficient tables, no data-availability statement or access pathway, no code, and a fall/spring outcome adjustment that underlies every main figure yet is specified only in an unavailable appendix.
- Positioning problems a reader may inherit: the novelty claim ("unlike other studies that focus on a single institution") is contradicted by the statewide and national studies the paper itself cites; the female result is uncontextualized and runs against the cited literature; grade-inflation, test-optional, and corequisite-remediation literatures bearing directly on the outcome and subgroup definitions are absent; and the reference list carries a wrong DOI (Rodríguez-Planas 2022b) and a misspelled author (Polikoff).

#### What to Rely On

- The Spring 2020 rise in four-year successful completion (about +5 pp) and earned credits (about +0.75) as grading-policy incidence, not improved learning — pass-type grades rose from roughly 1.5% to over 11% of courses and withdrawals stayed flat.
- The Spring 2020 community-college withdrawal/incomplete spike (about +11 pp) offset by fewer D/F grades (about −9 pp), aligned with the NCCCS emergency-grade guidance and replicating Bulman and Fairlie (2022) in a second state.
- The timing of the four-year decline: the largest drops in earned credits (about −0.5 to −0.6) and completion (about −2 to −3 pp) came with the 2021 high school cohort in 2021–22, after the acute disruption, with aggregate completion back near baseline for the 2022 cohort.
- The sector contrast in mechanism: four-year declines ran through D/F grades with essentially flat withdrawals; community-college declines ran through withdrawals and incompletes and through more students attending part-time.
- Fall-to-spring persistence fell about 1.5–2 pp at four-year institutions (against a 95% baseline) and about 3.5 pp at community colleges for the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, returning to trend for the class of 2022 at four-year institutions.
- Relative gaps in successful completion widened for students with below-median high school GPA — the largest and most robust subgroup finding (roughly 5–9 pp at four-year institutions in 2021–22, still around 5 pp at the end of the sample), and by 2–4 pp for URE, economically disadvantaged, and female students in the 2021 and 2022 cohorts — stated as widening gaps relative to the comparison group.
- Four-year summer enrollment rose about 5 pp from summer 2020 onward and stayed elevated — as a durable level shift in summer coursetaking, not as demonstrated credit recovery.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Declines have persisted" / "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for URE, economically disadvantaged, low-GPA, and female students — Figure 4 shows relative-to-reference-group differences only; the reference trajectories are unreported, so the level claim is reconstructed by the reader, not shown.
- The female-student finding as an established pattern — it is the smallest subgroup coefficient (about 2–3 pp, male-referenced), has no mechanism or literature behind it, runs against the cited evidence on male disadvantage, and may reflect the rising female share in the 2020–21 cohorts.
- The community-college decline as a pandemic effect — RISE moved weaker students into the credit-bearing courses the analysis retains over 2019–2021, no specification holds course mix fixed, and the final Spring 2023 completion and withdrawal points are at or above baseline.
- Any "recovery" read from spring semesters or from the right edge of the figures — spring samples condition on fall-to-spring persistence that fell during the pandemic, and later-cohort rebounds say nothing about the recovery of the cohorts that were hit.
- The below-median-GPA subgroup as a fixed preparation group — within-cohort rank neutralizes the documented scale and AP/IB weighting changes but not pandemic-era high school grade inflation or the UNC System's test-optional shift.
- The summer credit-recovery mechanism — explicitly untested (footnote 5), summer credits were flat conditional on enrolling, and the largest summer increase follows 2019–20, the year four-year credit earning rose.
- Specific magnitudes and the four-year confidence intervals — no coefficient is printed anywhere, 16 clusters with no small-sample correction make the four-year bands optimistic, and the fall/spring outcome adjustment underlying every figure is specified only in the Online Appendix.
- Any causal reading of the pandemic's effect — there is no untreated comparison group, and the authors state they cannot separate the pandemic from concurrent economic, policy, and political shocks.
- Generalization beyond first-year, immediately enrolling graduates of North Carolina public high schools at in-state public institutions — gap-year and delayed enrollees, private and out-of-state institutions, and outcomes past the first year are all excluded, and the abstract's "all ... high school graduates" overstates the sample.
- The paper's own novelty framing — do not repeat "unlike other studies that focus on a single institution"; Bird et al. (2022), Bulman and Fairlie (2022), and Howell et al. (2021, 2022) are multi-institution studies the paper itself cites. Cite it instead for the linked K-12-to-college records, the two-sector comparison, and the horizon through 2022–23.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a competently executed descriptive event study on unusually complete linked K-12/postsecondary administrative data for an entire state, and the authors are appropriately candid that the design has no untreated comparison group and cannot separate the pandemic from concurrent shocks. The core descriptive facts — a Spring 2020 grading-policy artifact, a real dip in credit earning and completion for the 2021 (and at community colleges, 2020-2022) cohorts, and wider relative gaps for lower-GPA, URE, economically disadvantaged, and female students — are large enough to survive the caveats. But three unaddressed threats (the RISE/developmental-education composition change at community colleges, endogenous selection into the observed sample and into the spring semester, and inference from 16 four-year clusters) constrain several specific claims, and the headline "have not recovered to baseline levels" is a claim about levels that Figure 4 does not actually display.

**Strengths:**

- Data coverage is a genuine strength: course-level transcripts for the near-universe of NC public high school graduates who enrolled immediately in-state (210,008 UNC and 192,793 NCCCS students), linked to NCDPI K-12 records. Because roughly 80% of immediate enrollers attend an in-state public institution, coverage problems are far smaller than in single-institution studies (Bird et al., Rodriguez-Planas) and there is no survey nonresponse.
- The paper is honest about its own inferential limits in the right places: the Conclusion states plainly that the study "is largely descriptive because all students were similarly exposed," and the Subgroup Differences section explicitly warns that a negative Equation 2 coefficient "does not necessarily mean that the outcome decreased for the given subgroup." That warning is exactly the right one and is unusual to see stated.
- Outcome decomposition is well designed and does real analytic work. Reporting attempted credits, earned credits, share completed with C or better, and share withdrawn/incomplete side by side lets the reader see mechanism rather than just magnitude — Figure 1 shows the 4-year Spring 2020 completion jump (+5pp, panel c) came with flat withdrawals (panel d), pinning it on avoided D/F grades; Figure 2 shows the mirror-image 2-year story, where the Spring 2020 +11pp withdrawal spike (panel d) offsets a 9pp drop in D/F. The two sectors are diagnosed as different phenomena because the decomposition allows it.
- Seasonal adjustment using prepandemic fall-spring differences, plus high school and postsecondary institution fixed effects, is a sensible way to keep the event-study coefficients from being contaminated by semester seasonality and by shifts in which schools and campuses students come from.
- Measurement threats are anticipated rather than hidden: footnote 2 documents both the 7-to-10-point scale change and the 2019 AP/IB weight change and explains the move to within-cohort GPA rank; footnote 4 quantifies the Pass/Satisfactory share rising from ~1.5% to over 11% in Spring 2020; the RISE program and its 2019-2021 timing are named in the Data Source section.

**Weaknesses:**

- The developmental-education exclusion collides with RISE in a way the main text acknowledges but does not resolve. Excluding dev-ed courses while RISE (implemented 2019-2020, paused 2021) was moving weaker community college students out of dev ed and into credit-bearing gateway math and English means the *set of courses* entering the 2-year analytic sample changed at almost exactly the pandemic onset — newly included gateway courses taken by students who previously would have been in excluded remedial sections. That mechanically depresses the "C or better" share and inflates withdrawals at 2-year institutions after 2019, independent of COVID. Footnote 6 addresses only the pre-2019 offset in attempted credits, not the post-2019 composition of the retained course pool. This is the most serious live confound for the entire Figure 2 story.
- Sample membership is itself an outcome. The analytic sample is conditional on graduating high school and enrolling immediately in an in-state public institution — and enrollment fell during exactly the study window, differentially so: footnote 3 reports that the 2-year enrollment drop "was most pronounced for low-achievement and economically disadvantaged students and for English language learners," and that top-quartile-GPA graduates shifted toward 2-year institutions after 2020. Covariate adjustment and high school fixed effects cannot fix selection on unobservables operating on the same margin as the outcome. The likely direction is attenuation: the weakest community college enrollees are missing from the post-2020 cohorts, so both the aggregate declines and the subgroup gaps in Figure 2 and Figure 4 are plausibly conservative — but the sign is not guaranteed, and the 4-year composition shift runs the other way.
- Spring-semester estimates condition on having persisted through the fall, and persistence itself fell. Figure 3a and 3b show fall-to-spring persistence declines of roughly 1.5-2pp at 4-year and 3.5pp at 2-year in the 2020-2021 cohorts, which means the spring samples in Figures 1, 2, and 4 are increasingly positively selected in precisely the pandemic semesters. This is the most natural explanation for the pronounced sawtooth visible in Figure 2c and 2b — fall coefficients consistently more negative than the following spring (2-year completion: about -0.055 in Fall 2021-22 versus -0.01 in Spring 2021-22; about -0.025 in Fall 2022-23 versus about +0.01 in Spring 2022-23). The seasonal adjustment is estimated on prepandemic data and by construction cannot absorb a survivorship pattern that only emerged after 2020, so the apparent spring "recovery" points are the least trustworthy in the paper.
- The headline "have not recovered to their baseline levels" is a statement about levels, but Figure 4 plots only the interaction coefficients from Equation 2 — differences relative to the reference group's own change. The level change for a subgroup is the sum of the two coefficients, and the reference-group coefficient is never shown. So a reader cannot verify from any exhibit in the paper that URE, economically disadvantaged, female, or below-median-GPA students remain below their own 2019 baseline; they can only verify that these groups fell further behind their comparison groups. The authors state the distinction correctly in the Subgroup Differences section, and then the Abstract and Introduction blur it.
- Inference at 4-year institutions rests on 16 clusters. Cluster-robust standard errors are downward biased well above that count, and no wild-cluster bootstrap, small-G correction, or randomization inference is reported. Every 4-year confidence interval — Figures 1, 3a, 3c, and the four-year series in Figure 4 — should be read as narrower than warranted, which matters most for the borderline claims (the not-significant Fall 2020 earned-credits increase, the near-zero end-of-sample points, and the smaller subgroup coefficients around -0.02).
- Pre-trends are visibly non-flat in several panels and no formal pre-trend test is reported. In Figure 2a and 2b (2-year attempted and earned credits) the pre-period rises from roughly -0.45 and -0.3 in Fall 2015-16 toward zero by 2018-19; in Figure 3b (2-year persistence) it falls from +0.024 to 0; in Figure 3d (2-year summer enrollment) it rises steeply from -0.05 to 0. When the counterfactual is a trend rather than a flat line, "relative to the preexisting trend" becomes a judgment call, and it is being made by eye.
- The within-cohort GPA rank fix is only a partial fix. Rank is invariant to the scale and weight changes footnote 2 describes, but not to pandemic-era changes in *high school grading practice* (leniency, hold-harmless, pass/fail options) that compressed and reshuffled the distribution non-monotonically across student types. The "below-median high school GPA" group in the 2020-2022 cohorts is therefore not the same latent-preparation group as in 2015-2018 — which bears directly on Figure 4a, the largest and most-emphasized subgroup result.
- The Spring 2020 coefficients are policy measurements, not learning measurements, and the outcome definition partly determines their sign. Counting "Satisfactory," "Pass," and "High Pass" as successful completion is a defensible choice, but at 4-year institutions it is what produces the +0.055 completion spike and the +0.75-credit jump in Figure 1b and 1c; coding those grades as non-successful would flip the finding. No alternative coding is shown in the main text.
- The summer credit-recovery claim is the weakest in the paper and is asserted more confidently than the evidence allows. Footnote 5 concedes the authors "do not test directly whether the summer enrollment is in classes that a student withdrew from or failed." More tellingly, Figure 3c shows 4-year summer enrollment jumping about 5pp in 2019-20 and staying at roughly that level through 2022-23, while the credit shortfall it is supposed to be remediating had largely closed by 2022-23. A make-up mechanism should track the deficit; a persistent level shift is more consistent with expanded online summer offerings or aid changes.
- Scale of multiple comparisons goes unacknowledged: six outcomes, two sectors, roughly sixteen event-time coefficients each, and four subgroup splits, with no adjustment and no joint tests. Point-in-time claims such as the "sharp drop for the lower-performing group in the fall of 2021" are drawn from that large family of coefficients.
- The share-based outcomes weight students equally regardless of course load, and the paper documents that part-time attendance rose at 2-year institutions after 2020 (Figure B2). A student taking one course and a student taking five contribute equally to the "share completed with C or better" mean, so a compositional shift toward light loads changes the measure even when per-course performance is fixed.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Figure 4 as evidence about *gaps*, not levels. The plotted coefficients are subgroup-minus-reference-group differences in change from Spring 2019. Coefficients of roughly -0.02 to -0.03 for URE (4a is GPA; 4b is URE), economically disadvantaged (4c), and female (4d) students, and -0.05 to -0.075 for below-median-GPA students (4a), support "these groups fell further behind" — they do not by themselves establish "these groups are still below their own 2019 level." If you need the level claim, you need the unreported reference-group coefficients from Equation 2; do not cite the Abstract's level phrasing as if Figure 4 showed it.
- Treat the aggregate 4-year "recovery" as reasonably well supported and the aggregate 2-year "persistent decline" as less so than the text implies. In Figure 1b and 1c the 4-year trough is the 2021-22 academic year (earned credits about -0.57 and -0.50; completion about -0.030 and -0.023) with the 2022-23 points back near zero. But in Figure 2 the final Spring 2022-23 points also return to roughly zero for completion (about +0.01), withdrawals (about +0.005), and earned credits (about -0.1, interval spanning zero). The "downward trends persisted" framing rests on the fall semesters and on the middle cohorts, not on the last observation.
- Discount the spring-semester coefficients relative to the fall ones throughout. Spring outcomes are conditional on having persisted from the fall, and Figure 3 shows persistence fell 1.5-2pp (4-year) and about 3.5pp (2-year) in the pandemic cohorts. Spring points are therefore drawn from a more positively selected sample in exactly the periods of interest, which biases them toward zero and inflates any "recovery" read off the right edge of the figures.
- Do not build on the 2-year results without first checking the Online Appendix developmental-education figures (B4 and the RISE discussion). Because remedial courses are excluded from the analytic sample and RISE moved weaker students out of remedial courses and into the credit-bearing courses that *are* in the sample over 2019-2020, an unknown share of the 2-year completion decline and withdrawal increase is a course-composition artifact rather than a pandemic effect. Verify whether the pattern survives including dev-ed courses or holding the course mix fixed before treating the community college finding as a COVID finding.
- Treat every Spring 2020 estimate as a measurement of grading policy. The 4-year +5pp completion jump and +0.75 earned credits (Figure 1b, 1c), the 2-year +11pp withdrawal spike and -9pp D/F drop (Figure 2c, 2d), and the Spring 2020 subgroup reversals in Figure 4a and 4b (lower-GPA and URE students doing relatively *better*) are all consistent with flexible grading (P/S grades rose from ~1.5% to >11% at 4-year campuses) rather than with changes in learning. Cite them as policy incidence, not as pandemic impacts on achievement.
- Widen the 4-year confidence intervals in your head. With 16 UNC clusters and no small-G correction, marginal 4-year results should not be treated as decisive — particularly the near-zero 2022-23 endpoints (which support "recovery") and the smaller subgroup coefficients around -0.02. The 2-year estimates (58 clusters) are on firmer inferential ground.
- Do not treat Figure 3d (2-year summer enrollment) as informative about the pandemic. Its pre-period rises monotonically from about -0.05 to 0 and the post-period continues upward to about +0.045; almost the entire pattern is trend extrapolation. Figure 3c (4-year summer, flat pre-period then a sharp ~5pp step) is the interpretable panel — but read it as a durable level shift in summer-taking, not as verified credit recovery, since the elevated summer enrollment persists after the credit deficit closes and no test links summer courses to previously failed or withdrawn ones.
- When comparing the below-median-GPA subgroup across cohorts, remember that the classifier itself moved. Within-cohort rank neutralizes the documented GPA scale and AP/IB weight changes but not pandemic-era shifts in high school grading practice, so the 2020-2022 "academically weaker" group is not a like-for-like match to the 2015-2018 one. Figure 4a is the paper's largest subgroup result and also its most measurement-fragile.
- Read the event-study x-axis as a sequence of different cohorts, not as a panel following students. Each cohort contributes exactly one fall and one spring of first-year data, so cohort and event time are collinear; every movement across the figure is a between-cohort comparison, and Table 1 shows composition moving (rising Hispanic, ELL, and disability shares that begin with the 2019 cohort and thus predate COVID). Covariates and high school fixed effects adjust for observed shifts only.
- Take the paper at the authors' own valuation, which is the correct one: this is high-quality descriptive documentation of what happened to NC public postsecondary cohorts, not an estimate of the causal effect of the pandemic. Any causal reading has to contend with the 2021-22 labor market, HEERF emergency aid, RISE, and institution-level policy changes, none of which can be separated from the cohort effects.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Design. Equations 1 and 2 are a cohort-by-semester event study with no untreated comparison group; identification rests entirely on the comparability of the 2015-2018 cohorts to the 2019-2022 cohorts after covariate and fixed-effect adjustment. The authors say this explicitly in the Conclusion and I would not penalize the paper for the choice — no credible control group exists for a universal shock, and the descriptive framing is the right one for Educational Researcher. What matters for readers is that the design's limits are respected in how specific numbers are cited, and the Abstract and Introduction do not consistently do that.

A structural feature worth naming: because the sample is restricted to first-year students enrolling immediately after high school, each cohort contributes exactly one fall and one spring. Semester and cohort are therefore collinear, and the alpha_t vector is a sequence of cohort effects. There is no within-student variation and no repeated observation of the same individuals across the event window. That is fine for the descriptive question, but it means every apparent "trend" or "recovery" is a comparison across different groups of people, which puts the entire weight of the exercise on the composition adjustment.

Composition. Table 1 shows the adjustment has real work to do and that some of the movement is not pandemic-driven. At 4-year institutions, ELL share more than doubles from 0.030 (2018) to 0.063 (2019) — before COVID — and Hispanic share rises monotonically from 0.063 to 0.091 across the window. At 2-year institutions the economically disadvantaged share peaks at 0.614 in 2019 and then falls to 0.578 by 2022, i.e. the community college sample becomes *less* disadvantaged in exactly the years the outcomes deteriorate. Footnote 3 confirms the mechanism: 2-year enrollment fell most for low-achievement, economically disadvantaged, and ELL students, while top-quartile-GPA graduates shifted toward 2-year institutions. Both movements imply the observed 2-year decline is measured on a *positively* selected post-2020 sample, so the aggregate declines in Figure 2 and the subgroup gaps in Figure 4 are probably conservative. That is the reassuring direction — but it is a conjecture about unobservables, not something the design demonstrates, and the 4-year composition shift runs the opposite way.

The RISE confound. This is the issue I would most want resolved before relying on the community college results. The analytic sample excludes developmental education courses. RISE was implemented 2019-2020 and paused in 2021, and its explicit purpose was to place students who would previously have taken remedial coursework directly into credit-bearing math and English. The excluded-course boundary therefore moved at the same moment as the treatment, and it moved in a direction that pulls weaker students' course attempts *into* the analytic sample. That mechanically lowers the "C or better" share and raises the withdrawal share at 2-year institutions after 2019. Footnote 6 tells us the pre-2019 rise in attempted credits was offset by falling dev-ed credits, which is a pre-period check, not a post-period one. The main text shows no specification with dev-ed included or with the course mix held fixed. Given that the sustained 2-year withdrawal increase is the paper's signature community college finding, this deserved more than an appendix figure.

Survivorship into spring. The most visually striking unaddressed pattern is the sawtooth in Figure 2. In 2c, completion runs about -0.055 in Fall 2021-22 versus about -0.01 in the following spring, and about -0.025 in Fall 2022-23 versus about +0.01 in Spring 2022-23; 2b shows the same alternation. Fall and spring within an academic year are the same cohort, so a within-year zigzag of this size cannot be composition across cohorts. The natural explanation is that the spring sample is conditional on fall persistence, which Figure 3b shows fell about 3.5pp in 2020-21 and 2.8pp in 2021-22 at community colleges. The seasonal adjustment is estimated off prepandemic fall-spring differences and so cannot absorb a selection pattern that only appeared after 2020. This directly undercuts any reading of the rightmost spring points as evidence of recovery, in both sectors.

Levels versus gaps. The Subgroup Differences section states the interpretation correctly — "A negative coefficient estimate does not necessarily mean that the outcome decreased for the given subgroup" — and then the Abstract says "These declines have persisted for certain groups" and the Introduction says success rates "have not recovered to their baseline levels for students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, economically disadvantaged and academically weaker students, and females." Those are level claims. Figure 4 plots beta_t^1 only. The level change for a subgroup is beta_t^0 + beta_t^1, and beta_t^0 appears in no exhibit. Working from Figure 1c, the 4-year aggregate at Spring 2022-23 is roughly +0.005, so the non-URE reference group sits slightly above that, and a URE beta^1 of about -0.02 would put URE students modestly below their own baseline — plausible, but reconstructed by the reader, not shown. The below-median-GPA case is stronger (4-year beta^1 reaching about -0.075 in Fall 2021-22 and about -0.05 in Fall 2022-23; 2-year triangles around -0.05 to -0.06 in the last two cohorts) and probably does survive the level translation. The female and economically disadvantaged claims, at roughly -0.02 to -0.03, are the ones where "fell behind the reference group" and "did not recover" can genuinely come apart.

Inference. Clustering at the postsecondary institution is the right level for serial correlation within campus, but G = 16 at UNC is far below where cluster-robust asymptotics are trustworthy, and no wild bootstrap or small-G correction is mentioned. All 4-year intervals should be read as too narrow. Separately, the family of reported coefficients is very large — six outcomes, two sectors, about sixteen event-time points, four subgroup splits — with no multiplicity adjustment and no joint tests, so single-semester claims such as the Fall 2021 drop for low-GPA students are selected from a wide field. And no formal pre-trend test is reported anywhere, despite Figures 2a, 2b, 3b, and 3d having visibly sloped pre-periods.

Measurement. Two issues compound. First, the "C or better" outcome is defined to include Satisfactory/Pass/High Pass, and footnote 4 tells us those grades went from ~1.5% to over 11% of 4-year courses in Spring 2020 — so the +5pp Spring 2020 completion spike and much of the +0.75 earned-credit jump are the grading policy, and an alternative coding would reverse the sign. The authors interpret this correctly, but readers should not carry the number forward as an achievement estimate. Second, within-cohort GPA rank protects against the documented scale and AP/IB weight changes (footnote 2) but not against pandemic-era changes in high school grading practice, which reshuffled the distribution non-monotonically. Since Figure 4a is the largest subgroup effect, the group whose definition is least stable is also the one carrying the most weight.

What is load-bearing and what is not. Firm: (i) 4-year successful completion and earned credits spiked in Spring 2020 and this was a grading-policy artifact; (ii) 2-year withdrawals spiked 11pp in Spring 2020 with an offsetting 9pp drop in D/F grades, mirroring Bulman and Fairlie's California finding; (iii) 4-year credit earning fell substantially for the 2021 cohort (about -0.5 to -0.6 credits, -2 to -3pp completion) and had largely returned to baseline by 2022-23; (iv) fall-to-spring persistence fell about 1.5-2pp at 4-year and 3.5pp at 2-year for the 2020-2021 cohorts, which is material against a 95% 4-year baseline; (v) relative gaps in successful completion widened for below-median-GPA, URE, economically disadvantaged, and female students in the 2021-2022 cohorts. Contestable: (a) the community college decline as a *pandemic* effect, given RISE; (b) "have not recovered to baseline levels" for the subgroups, which is a level claim the figures do not display and which the last spring observation partially contradicts in aggregate; (c) the persistence of the 2-year decline, which weakens sharply at the final Spring 2022-23 point in three of four Figure 2 panels; (d) the summer credit-recovery mechanism, which is temporal correlation only, is explicitly untested in footnote 5, and is undercut by the +5pp 4-year summer level persisting through 2022-23 after the credit deficit had closed.

Assessment. Adequate, on the high end. The design suits the descriptive question, the data are excellent, the outcome decomposition is genuinely illuminating, and the authors flag most of the right caveats. It falls short of strong because identification is purely temporal with non-flat pre-trends and no formal pre-trend testing; because the two most consequential confounds (RISE course-composition and endogenous sample selection) are named but never probed in the main text; because inference at 4-year institutions rests on 16 clusters without correction; and because the framing of the central subgroup claim outruns what the exhibits show. None of that undermines the paper's core contribution, which is a careful description of what happened to a state's entire immediate-enrollment population.

Confidence note: this assessment worked from the complete main text and all four figures at legible resolution, but Online Appendix A (empirical detail) and Appendix B (roughly sixteen subgroup and robustness figures, plus baseline descriptives in B1 and the enrollment-shift evidence in B2 and dev-ed trends in B4) were not available. Several of the cautions above — especially on RISE, on part-time composition, and on whether subgroup patterns replicate across the other five outcomes — are exactly the things those appendices may already address.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The Background is wide-ranging and correctly identifies the paper's closest antecedents — the early-pandemic postsecondary studies (Bird et al., Bulman & Fairlie, Rodríguez-Planas, Aucejo et al., Howell et al.) and the small recent recovery literature (Westrick et al., Kuperman et al., Dagorn & Moulin) — and it usefully situates the work against the much larger K-12 learning-loss evidence base. But its central novelty claim ("unlike other studies that focus on a single institution") is inaccurate against multi-institution studies the paper itself cites two paragraphs earlier; several load-bearing comparison points are non-peer-reviewed College Board reports or the authors' own unpublished working papers; there are concrete reference-list errors; and the paper does not engage the grade-inflation, test-optional, developmental-education-reform, or gender literatures that bear directly on its own headline findings.

**Strengths:**

- The set of early-pandemic postsecondary studies is the right one and is described with unusual specificity: Bird et al. (2022) on the Virginia Community College System, Bulman & Fairlie (2022) on California community colleges, Rodríguez-Planas (2022a/b) on CUNY/Queens College, Aucejo et al. (2020) on Arizona State. A reader looking for the canonical spring-2020 postsecondary papers will find them here.
- The paper does not stop at 2020-2022 work. It reaches for the thin recovery literature — Westrick et al. (2024) on first-year GPA by institutional selectivity, Kuperman et al. (2026) on Canadian grade inflation and its partial reversal, Dagorn & Moulin (2025) on French reenrollment — which is more than most postsecondary COVID papers do and is exactly the literature a reader needs to triangulate the paper's own longer-horizon claim.
- The Background is organized around mechanisms rather than a chronological citation dump: K-12 preparation effects, compositional change in who enrolls, online-learning effectiveness, grading-policy change, and non-academic shocks (health, mental health, income, connectivity). This structure makes it easy for a reader to see which prior literatures speak to which part of the observed pattern.
- It engages the online-learning literature honestly as genuinely mixed (Bettinger et al. 2017 negative; Means et al. 2013 positive; Altindag et al. 2025 on a narrowing gap since 2020) rather than cherry-picking the direction that suits the story.
- The paper correctly foregrounds Fuller et al. (2025), the closest North Carolina K-12 antecedent in the same journal, which gives readers a natural upstream companion for the high school side of the same cohorts.
- Grading-policy confounding is flagged in the literature discussion up front (Day et al. 2021; NCCCS WE/IE codes; UNC System pass/satisfactory options), not buried as a limitation — so a reader is warned before seeing the spring-2020 spike.

**Weaknesses:**

- The novelty claim is not accurate as written. "Unlike other studies that focus on a single institution, the trends we uncover are representative of a wide range of postsecondary institutions" is contradicted by the paper's own preceding paragraph: Bird et al. (2022) covers the entire 23-college Virginia Community College System, Bulman & Fairlie (2022) covers the ~116-college California system, and Howell et al. (2021, 2022) use national College Board/Clearinghouse data. The single-institution foil fits only Aucejo et al. (ASU), Rodríguez-Planas (Queens College), and Kuperman et al. (two Canadian universities). The genuinely novel elements — the linked K-12-to-postsecondary records that supply high school GPA and economic-disadvantage measures, coverage of the 2- and 4-year sectors on identical measures, and the extension through the class of 2022 — are real but are described in the weakest available terms.
- "Representative of a wide range of postsecondary institutions" also oversells external validity in a second way: the sample is one state's public system, with no private, no selective-private, and no out-of-state institutions, and it conditions on immediate enrollment. That is a broad within-state sample, not a nationally representative one.
- Three of the paper's key comparison points — Howell et al. (2021), Howell et al. (2022), and Westrick et al. (2024) — are non-peer-reviewed research reports from a single organization (College Board), and this is nowhere signaled. Two more load-bearing citations (Eilam et al. 2026 on enrollment and composition; Hutchins et al. 2026 on advisors encouraging lighter courseloads) are the authors' own unpublished working papers with no URL, venue, or institution given. A reader cannot check the compositional-change premise or the lighter-courseload mechanism from anything in the public record.
- Direct conflicting evidence is cited but never reconciled. Westrick et al. (2024) report first-year GPA increases for the classes of 2020 and 2021 at more selective institutions with declines only at less selective ones; Kuperman et al. (2026) report grades still elevated in 2023 in some faculties. The UNC System spans a wide selectivity range, yet the paper reports post-2021 declines without asking whether the discrepancy is about selectivity composition, outcome definition (share of courses at C-or-better versus mean GPA), or state-specific grading policy. The Background sets up the tension and then drops it.
- There is no engagement with the grade-inflation and lowered-standards literature, despite the outcome being a grade-threshold measure (C or better) and despite the paper's own spring-2020 spike being explicitly attributed to flexible grading. Denning, Eide, Mumford, Patterson & Warnick (2022, AEJ: Applied) — which attributes rising college completion largely to grading standards rather than student preparation or institutional resources — is the obvious missing anchor, along with the general grade-inflation trend work. Kuperman et al. (2026) is cited but treated as a data point about levels, not as an entry into that literature.
- The high school GPA inflation problem is acknowledged only as a North Carolina weighting-policy change (7-point to 10-point scale; AP/IB weight reduction), not as a substantive literature. The paper's "below-median high school GPA" subgroup is a central heterogeneity cut, yet the well-documented pandemic-era grade inflation in high schools — which makes a given GPA rank a different signal of preparation across cohorts — is neither cited nor discussed. Readers should not read the below-median subgroup as holding preparation fixed across cohorts.
- Test-optional admissions goes uncited entirely. The UNC System suspended test requirements for pandemic-era cohorts, which is a first-order driver of exactly the compositional change the paper worries about and of what "academically weaker" means in these cohorts. The relevant empirical literature on test-optional adoption and enrollment composition is absent.
- The paper names RISE (Reinforced Instruction for Student Excellence) as a North Carolina developmental-education reform that overlapped the pandemic and directly moved students into credit-bearing math and English, but cites no corequisite-remediation or developmental-education-reform literature at all. For the 2-year results — where credit-earning and withdrawal trends are the headline — this is the most serious substantive omission, because the reform and the pandemic are confounded and the reader is given no external evidence base for how large corequisite effects on course completion typically are.
- The finding that female students recovered more slowly is one of the paper's four headline heterogeneity results and has essentially no literature behind it. Nothing in the Background predicts it, and it cuts against the pattern in cited work (Ross et al. 2012 on lower male persistence; Bulman & Fairlie's larger declines for men). The adolescent-mental-health literature showing sharper pandemic deterioration for girls, and the pandemic caregiving-burden literature, are both absent. Readers get a striking result with no scholarly context for interpreting it.
- National Student Clearinghouse Research Center work is cited once for a background persistence statistic but is never used as a benchmark. Its cohort persistence and retention series is the natural national yardstick for whether North Carolina's trajectory is typical or distinctive, and the community-college enrollment collapse and partial rebound documented there is directly relevant to the composition story.
- Other state administrative-data studies of post-pandemic college outcomes are not surveyed. The paper's implicit claim that this kind of linked-records, multi-sector state analysis is unprecedented would be more credible if it engaged the state-longitudinal-data-system work that exists in other states.
- Concrete reference-list errors. (1) Rodríguez-Planas (2022b) is listed in Economics of Education Review 87, Article 102233, but the DOI given is 10.1016/j.jpubeco.2022.104606 — a Journal of Public Economics identifier that in fact resolves to the 2022a article. (2) The name is spelled "Polikof" in the Introduction and in the reference list but "Polikoff" in the Conclusion; the correct spelling is Polikoff. (3) "Aera Open" should be AERA Open, and the Bird et al. entry is out of alphabetical order (placed after Braxton). (4) Betthäuser et al. is in Nature Human Behaviour, not "Nature Human Behavior."
- "Jack et al. (2023)" is cited in the opening sentence for the timing and duration of school closures. That paper (Jack, Halloran, Okun & Oster, AERI) is about schooling mode and test scores; it does document instruction-mode shares, so the citation is defensible but not the natural source for closure timing, and it is then cited again a page later for the learning-loss result. A reader tracking claim-to-source should note the same citation is doing two different jobs.
- Much of the Background is a catalogue of mechanisms the study cannot test — COVID infection risk disparities, mental health, online racial discrimination, parental constraints, internet access. These citations are accurate but create an implied explanatory frame that the descriptive event study never adjudicates. The literature review is considerably broader than the paper's evidentiary reach.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not cite this paper as the first multi-institution evidence on pandemic-era college performance. Cite Bird, Castleman & Lohner (2022) and Bulman & Fairlie (2022) for statewide community-college systems in spring 2020, and Howell et al. (2021, 2022) for national enrollment and persistence. Cite Gicheva et al. for what is actually distinctive: linked high school and college administrative records in one state, both sectors on identical outcome definitions, extending through the class of 2022 and fall 2022.
- Verify before repeating the specific numbers attributed to prior work. Check Bird et al. (2022) for the 2.7-point withdrawal and 1.3-point failure figures and for whether those are the headline estimates or components of a larger course-completion effect; check Howell et al. (2022) for the 2.6-point 4-year public persistence decline and the subgroup direction; and check Howell et al. (2021) for the claim that 4-year enrollment declines fell primarily on White and Asian students, students with BA-holding parents, and the highest-GPA students. That last claim is the paper's basis for its compositional-change premise and runs against the more commonly cited pattern of steeper declines at high-poverty and high-minority high schools, so it is worth confirming which population and which comparison it refers to.
- Note that Howell et al. (2021), Howell et al. (2022), and Westrick et al. (2024) are all College Board research reports, not peer-reviewed articles, and that the Polikoff et al. (2023) call-to-action and Lewis & Kuhfeld (2023) are also gray literature. This is normal in the pandemic-education literature given publication lags, but it means several of the paper's benchmarks have not been refereed.
- Treat the two 2026 working papers by the same team (Eilam et al. on enrollment and persistence; Hutchins et al. on staff and student perceptions) as currently uncheckable. The lighter-courseload advising mechanism and the enrollment-composition results rest on them; if you need either claim, request the working papers directly from the authors.
- Read this alongside Denning, Eide, Mumford, Patterson & Warnick (2022, AEJ: Applied) on grading standards and completion, and alongside the general grade-inflation literature, before interpreting a C-or-better completion rate as a measure of learning. The paper's own spring-2020 spike is a grading-policy artifact by its own account; the same logic implies the later decline could partly reflect grading policies returning to normal rather than students learning less.
- Pair it with Westrick et al. (2024) deliberately, since that is the closest thing to a direct contradiction in the U.S. literature: GPA up at selective institutions, flat or down at less selective ones. The reconciliation the paper does not attempt — selectivity composition, GPA versus threshold-based completion, and state grading policy — is where a careful reader should focus.
- Supply the missing high-school-side context yourself. Pandemic-era high school grade inflation and the UNC System's test-optional shift both mean that "below-median high school GPA" identifies a differently constituted group in the 2020-2022 cohorts than in 2015-2018. The heterogeneity results by baseline achievement should be read as descriptive of a shifting group, not as holding preparation constant.
- For the 2-year results specifically, read the corequisite and developmental-education reform literature and North Carolina's own RISE documentation. RISE moved students out of developmental courses into credit-bearing math and English during 2019-2020 and was paused in 2021 — a policy shock that is confounded with the pandemic and moves the same outcomes in plausibly the same direction. The paper notes RISE but gives readers no external basis for gauging its magnitude.
- Benchmark the trends against National Student Clearinghouse Research Center persistence-and-retention and enrollment reports. Those series will tell you whether North Carolina's post-2021 decline and partial rebound track the national pattern or diverge from it, which is the question the paper's descriptive design cannot answer on its own.
- The slower recovery for female students is the finding most in need of outside context and is the one the paper supports least. Nothing in its Background anticipates it, and it runs against the cited literature on male disadvantage in persistence. Look to the adolescent and young-adult mental health literature (which documents sharper pandemic deterioration among girls and young women) and to the pandemic caregiving-burden literature before treating this as an established postsecondary pattern; treat it as a finding awaiting replication elsewhere.
- Two citation corrections to carry forward if you cite through this paper: the author of the CRPE consensus-panel report is Polikoff, not "Polikof"; and the Rodríguez-Planas (2022b) DOI printed in the reference list belongs to Rodríguez-Planas (2022a) in the Journal of Public Economics, not to the Economics of Education Review article. Pull both from the journals directly rather than from this reference list.
- Read the Background's mechanism catalogue (health disparities, discrimination, mental health, connectivity, parental constraints) as motivation rather than as findings. The event study identifies none of these channels, and the paper is explicit that it cannot separate the pandemic from concurrent economic and political shocks.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The scholarly positioning of this paper is competent but has one structural flaw and one pattern of omission that together should shape how readers use it.

The structural flaw is the novelty claim. The paper writes that "unlike other studies that focus on a single institution, the trends we uncover are representative of a wide range of postsecondary institutions." That sentence is directly contradicted by the paragraph immediately above it, which describes Bird et al. (2022) as covering the Virginia Community College System, Bulman & Fairlie (2022) as covering California administrative data, and Howell et al. (2022) as reporting national U.S. persistence patterns. None of those is a single institution. The single-institution studies in this literature are Aucejo et al. (Arizona State), Rodríguez-Planas (Queens College, CUNY), and Kuperman et al. (two Canadian universities) — all survey- or transcript-based studies of one campus, and the last is not U.S. The consequence for readers is not that the paper is unoriginal; it is that the paper misidentifies its own contribution. What is actually distinctive here is the combination of (a) K-12-to-postsecondary record linkage supplying pre-college GPA, economic disadvantage, EL and disability status for the full population, (b) parallel 2-year and 4-year analyses on identical outcome definitions within one state, and (c) a horizon reaching the high school class of 2022 and fall 2022 semester, well past the spring-2020 window most of the literature occupies. Those are the grounds on which the paper should be cited. The multi-versus-single-institution framing should not be repeated.

The pattern of omission is that the literatures most likely to explain the paper's own results are the ones absent. The outcome is share of courses completed with a C or better. That is a grading-standards measure, and the paper's headline spring-2020 result is explicitly a grading-policy artifact (flexible pass/satisfactory options at UNC institutions; WE and IE codes at NCCCS). Having established that grading policy drives the early spike, the paper does not then ask whether grading policy drives the later decline as policies unwound — and it cites none of the grade-inflation literature that would let a reader think about this, with Denning et al. (2022) the most conspicuous absence given that its whole argument is that completion measures track grading standards more than they track preparation. Similarly, the paper's baseline-achievement control and one of its four heterogeneity cuts rest on weighted high school GPA. It acknowledges two North Carolina policy changes affecting GPA and handles them by using within-cohort rank, but never raises pandemic-era high school grade inflation, and never mentions that the UNC System's move to test-optional admissions during exactly these cohorts changes both who enrolls and what a given GPA rank signals. Finally, for the 2-year results, the paper names RISE as a concurrent developmental-education reform affecting the same outcomes in the same years but cites no literature on corequisite remediation that would let a reader gauge how much of the community-college credit-earning shift RISE could account for.

On engagement with conflicting evidence, the paper deserves partial credit and no more. It cites Westrick et al. (2024) — first-year GPA up at more selective private institutions, up less at selective publics, flat or down at less selective ones — and Kuperman et al. (2026), which finds grades still elevated post-pandemic in humanities and social sciences. Both cut against this paper's post-2021 decline story, at least for parts of the institutional distribution. Having placed both on the table, the paper moves on without reconciling them. The reconciliation is not obvious: it could be selectivity composition (the UNC System includes both flagship and open-access institutions), outcome definition (a threshold-based completion share behaves differently from a mean GPA under grade compression), or genuine state variation in grading-policy unwinding. Readers should treat the fuller evidence base as showing a selectivity gradient in pandemic-era academic outcomes, with this paper contributing the mid-to-broad-access public segment, rather than as showing a uniform post-2021 decline.

The gender result deserves separate mention because it is the paper's least-supported headline. The finding that female students' successful completion recovered more slowly is presented in the abstract and conclusion, but no part of the Background anticipates it, and it runs contrary to the cited persistence literature (Ross et al. 2012) and to Bulman & Fairlie's community-college enrollment findings, where declines were more pronounced for men. Two adjacent literatures would have supplied context — the developmental and psychiatric evidence on sharper pandemic mental-health deterioration among adolescent girls and young women, and the pandemic caregiving-burden literature — and neither appears. A reader should treat this as an interesting, essentially uncontextualized descriptive finding.

On the evidentiary status of the sources: three of the paper's most-relied-upon comparison points (Howell et al. 2021, Howell et al. 2022, Westrick et al. 2024) are College Board research reports rather than refereed articles, and two more (Eilam et al. 2026; Hutchins et al. 2026) are the authors' own working papers with no venue or link. The working papers carry real weight — Eilam et al. supports the compositional-change discussion including the claim that top-quartile GPA graduates shifted toward 2-year institutions, and Hutchins et al. supplies the advising-toward-lighter-courseloads interpretation of declining attempted credits at community colleges. Neither can be checked. Gray literature is normal and often unavoidable in a literature this recent, but the concentration of it at the load-bearing points is worth knowing.

On reference accuracy: the Rodríguez-Planas (2022b) entry pairs an Economics of Education Review citation with a Journal of Public Economics DOI that resolves to Rodríguez-Planas (2022a). That is an unambiguous error and will misdirect anyone who follows the link. "Polikof" appears twice (Introduction and reference list) against "Polikoff" once (Conclusion); Polikoff is correct. "Aera Open" should be AERA Open, Bird et al. is out of alphabetical order, and Betthäuser et al. is in Nature Human Behaviour. The Jack et al. (2023) citation in the opening sentence, used for closure timing and duration, is a stretch for that specific claim — the paper is about schooling mode and test scores — though it does report instruction-mode shares, so it is defensible rather than wrong.

One broader observation about the shape of the Background. Roughly half of it catalogues mechanisms — COVID infection disparities, mental health, online racial discrimination, parental time constraints, internet access, peer composition — that the study's descriptive event study cannot test. Every citation is individually appropriate, and the section reads as a competent survey. But the effect is that the literature review promises explanatory reach the analysis does not deliver, and the conclusion is candid about this ("we are unable to disentangle the pandemic's impacts from the effects of other concurrent events and policies"). Readers should hold the Background and the Results at arm's length from each other: the former is a map of what could have mattered; the latter is a set of conditional means by cohort and semester.

A note on the limits of this assessment. The structure of the literature review, the internal consistency of its novelty claim against its own citations, and the presence or absence of major adjacent literatures can be evaluated from the text. Several of the cited works date from 2025 and 2026 — Kuperman et al., Dagorn & Moulin, Altindag et al., Katz et al., Fahle et al., Hanushek & Strauss, Fuller et al. — and their findings, and whether they are characterized correctly, could not be independently verified. The same caution applies to the specific numerical claims attributed to Bird et al., Bulman & Fairlie, and the two Howell reports: the descriptions are internally plausible and appropriately specific, but they are flagged for verification rather than asserted to be wrong. Readers who plan to repeat those numbers should pull the sources.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The prose is clean, compact, and well-organized for a 14-page ER feature, and most stated magnitudes check out precisely against the figures (0.75 credits, 5 pp, 9 pp, 11 pp, 1-2 pp all verify). The exposition breaks down in two places that matter for readers: the abstract and introduction convert Figure 4's relative-to-reference-group coefficients into claims about absolute declines that have "not recovered to their baseline levels," which no main-text exhibit can support; and the main text is not self-contained, deferring baseline levels for every outcome, the full-time/part-time decomposition, the D/F series, and subgroup results for five of six outcomes to an Online Appendix of roughly eighteen exhibits.

**Strengths:**

- Numerical fidelity in the Results section is genuinely good. Nearly every magnitude the prose states is verifiable in the figure it cites: the Spring 2020 earned-credit spike is +0.78 credits (text: "around 0.75 hours"); the Spring 2020 successful-completion jump at 4-year institutions is +0.054 (text: "around 5 percentage points"); the 2-year Spring 2020 withdrawal/incomplete spike is +0.109 (text: "11 percentage points"); the 4-year persistence dip is -0.017 in 2020-21 and -0.016 in 2021-22 (text: "a 1 to 2 percentage point decrease"). The "9 percentage point" D/F decrease at 2-year institutions is not plotted anywhere but is exactly recoverable from Figures 2c and 2d (-(-0.019) - 0.109 = -0.090), and the paper explicitly tells readers this residual "can be calculated by the reader."
- The paper anticipates its own most dangerous reader trap and warns about it in plain language before Figure 4: "A negative coefficient estimate does not necessarily mean that the outcome decreased for the given subgroup; it can indicate that the outcome increased by less than the increase for the relevant reference group." Equation 2's exposition is also unusually careful, spelling out that the total change for females is the sum of the reference-group coefficient and the interaction. This is better than most papers of this type do.
- The four figures are a consistent, well-designed system: identical x-axis conventions, matched y-axis ranges across the two credit-earning figures (so Figure 1 and Figure 2 are visually comparable panel-for-panel), consistent 95% CI presentation, and a clear circle/triangle 2-year-versus-4-year encoding with a legend in Figure 4. The figure notes are near-identical boilerplate that states sample size, reference period, seasonal adjustment, control set, and clustering level, so each figure is close to self-contained on methods.
- The Results section signposts its own qualification honestly. After concluding that 4-year credit earning "appears to have recovered," the text immediately adds "Later in this section, we show evidence that this is not the case for all students," and the Subgroup Differences section opens by naming the question. Anticipated inconsistencies between the overall-rebound and no-recovery-for-subgroups messages are therefore navigable, not accidental.
- Anticipated limitations are stated squarely and without hedging in the Conclusion: "our study is largely descriptive because all students were similarly exposed to the COVID-19 pandemic, so we are unable to disentangle the pandemic's impacts from the effects of other concurrent events and policies," with concrete confounders named (stimulus payments, unemployment, the 2020 racial-justice protests, and elsewhere the RISE developmental-education reform and the AP/IB GPA-weighting change).

**Weaknesses:**

- The abstract's central claim is not supportable from any main-text exhibit. It states "These declines have persisted for certain groups, including students from underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, economically disadvantaged and academically weaker students, as well as female students," and the Introduction sharpens this to declines that "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for those groups. But Figure 4 plots only the beta-1 interaction terms, i.e. the subgroup's deviation relative to its reference group's deviation. The reference-group coefficients (beta-0) are never reported anywhere in the main text, so the level trajectory for URE, economically disadvantaged, female, or low-GPA students cannot be reconstructed by a reader. Meanwhile Figures 1c and 2c show pooled successful completion essentially back to baseline by Spring 2023 (+0.006 at 4-year, +0.011 at 2-year). The paper flags this exact inference error before Figure 4 and then commits it in the abstract, the introduction, and the phrase "successful completion rates were lower for female, URE, and economically disadvantaged students."
- Several "sustained" and "persisting" characterizations are contradicted by the final data point of the very figure being described. The text concludes the 2-year section with "the decrease persisting for the later cohorts in our data. North Carolina community college students are less likely to complete classes, driven by a sustained increase in course withdrawals." Figure 2c's last point (Spring 2023) is approximately +0.011, above baseline, and Figure 2d's last point is approximately +0.007, effectively back to baseline. The 2-year series is also strongly non-monotone in a fall-versus-spring sawtooth (successful completion runs roughly -0.042, -0.012, -0.054, -0.009, -0.027, +0.011 across the six post-onset semesters), which the prose never mentions even though the figures claim to have already netted out prepandemic seasonality.
- The main text is not self-contained on magnitude. All four figures are plotted in deviations from a Spring 2019 or 2018-19 baseline, and baseline levels for every outcome are relegated to Table B1 in the Online Appendix. The only anchor offered anywhere in the body is the single sentence noting that the 4-year baseline persistence rate "was 95%." A reader of the print article therefore has no way to judge whether a 0.5-credit drop in earned credits or a 5-percentage-point shift in completion share is large, except for persistence. Roughly eighteen appendix exhibits (Appendix A on methods, Tables B1-B2, Figures B1-B16) carry material the main text relies on: the full-time/part-time decomposition that distinguishes the 4-year from the 2-year attempted-credit story, the D/F series, and subgroup results for five of the six outcomes.
- The summer-enrollment narrative does not fit its own figure's timing. The Introduction promises "evidence that some students at 4-year institutions may have used the summer semesters to recover credits they failed to earn during the preceding academic year," with a policy implication about summer course options. But the largest summer increase in Figure 3c is the first post-onset point, the summer following 2019-20 (approximately +0.067) - the same year in which 4-year earned credits rose by 0.78 and successful completion rose by 5 pp. There were no failed credits to recover that year. The paper concedes in Outcomes that "we do not test directly whether the summer enrollment is in classes that a student withdrew from or failed," and footnote 5 reports summer credits attempted and earned were flat conditional on enrolling. The Conclusion then drops the summer finding entirely, so a claim promoted to the Introduction's contribution list never returns.
- "Female" is carried in the abstract's headline vulnerable-groups list on the strength of a single clause of prose and never explained. Figure 4d does support a persistent relative gap (4-year approximately -0.021 to -0.025 in 2022-23, 2-year approximately -0.028 to -0.041), comparable in size to the URE gap in Figure 4b, so the inclusion is not unfounded. But the Background section sets up the opposite expectation, citing Ross et al. (2012) for "lower persistence rates for males," and the paper offers no mechanism, no engagement with that tension, and no discussion of whether the female gap reflects compositional shifts visible in Table 1 (the female share rose significantly in the 2020 and 2021 cohorts at 4-year institutions). It is the paper's most surprising result and its least explained.
- The dashed vertical line means different things across figures and does not match the treatment timing the text specifies. In Figures 1, 2, and 4 it falls between Fall 2019 and Spring 2020 (March 2020); in Figure 3 it falls between the 2018-19 and 2019-20 academic years. But the Outcomes section states that "for attempted credits and fall-to-spring persistence, the COVID-19 pandemic should not have been a factor until the fall of 2020." So in Figure 1a and Figure 3a the first one or two points to the right of the dashed line are actually pre-treatment, and nothing in the panel, its title, or its note says so. That caveat sits in a short paragraph at the end of Outcomes, four pages before Figure 3.
- The Spring 2019 reference period is rendered invisibly. In every panel the baseline is the eighth point, drawn at exactly zero with a confidence interval too small to see, and the x-axis labels only academic years with alternating F/S ticks. Nothing marks which tick is the omitted category, and Figure 3's x-axis drops the F/S ticks entirely so its baseline (2018-19) is a bare dot. Combined with the fact that the summer panels (3c, 3d) are labeled by the preceding academic year - so the point labeled "19-20" is summer 2020 - the x-axis takes real work to decode.
- Two smaller reader frictions. First, "about 0.25 credits per semester" for the attempted-credit decline in Figure 1a describes only the two largest post-onset points (-0.27); the eight post-onset estimates range from -0.03 to -0.27 and average roughly -0.16. The accompanying claim that the decline "appears to be a continuation of the preexisting trend" is asserted rather than tested, and the post-2020 slope in the figure is visibly steeper than the pre-2020 drift. Second, footnote 2 says the analyses "focus on a student's relative GPA rank within their cohort," while Table 1 reports raw weighted GPA and every figure note lists the control as "below-median high school grade point average"; these reconcile, but only after a beat.
- The abstract describes the sample as "administrative data on all 2015-2022 high school graduates in North Carolina who enrolled in an in-state public institution." The word "all" overstates: the sample is restricted to public high school graduates (private and home-schooled excluded via the NCDPI link) who enrolled immediately (gap-year students excluded), and the Setting section notes only about 80% of immediate enrollers attend an in-state public institution. Since footnote 3 and Table B2 report that enrollment patterns shifted by GPA and economic status after 2020, selection into the estimation sample changed over exactly the period being studied - a point the abstract omits, along with the study's descriptive, non-causal character.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the Results section with Figures 1 through 4 open beside it; the article is short enough that skipping straight to Results costs little, since the Background section is a conventional literature survey that does not set up any specific hypothesis the analysis tests. The load-bearing exhibits are Figure 1 (4-year credit earning), Figure 2 (2-year credit earning), and Figure 4 (subgroups). Figure 3 and Table 1 are supporting.
- Treat Figure 4 as the paper's single biggest trap and read the paragraph immediately preceding it before reading the figure. Every coefficient there is a difference-in-deviations relative to a reference group (males, non-URE, non-economically-disadvantaged, above-median GPA), and the reference group's own trajectory is never shown. Do not quote Figure 4 as evidence that any subgroup's completion rate fell; it licenses only the statement that gaps between groups widened and have not closed. Where the abstract, introduction, or the phrase "successful completion rates were lower for female, URE, and economically disadvantaged students" implies absolute decline, substitute "relative to the comparison group."
- Before citing the recovery finding, look at the last two points of each panel yourself. At 4-year institutions the successful-completion series (Figure 1c) does return to baseline (approximately -0.008 and +0.006 in 2022-23), but earned credits (Figure 1b) end at approximately -0.25 and -0.11, and attempted credits (Figure 1a) never recover at all (approximately -0.17 and -0.22). Because completion is a share of attempted credits, part of the apparent rebound in 1c coexists with students simply attempting less - a connection the prose does not draw. At 2-year institutions the final Spring 2023 points in Figures 2c and 2d are back at or above baseline, which sits awkwardly with the text's "sustained increase in course withdrawals."
- Note that "rebounded" throughout means a later cohort did better in its own first year, not that any affected student recovered. The design observes only first-year outcomes for each high school cohort, so the 2022-23 points describe the class of 2022, not the recovery of the class of 2021. The Conclusion states this ("it is yet unclear what the long-term trends would be for students who attended college at the height of the pandemic"), but only in its final clause; carry the caveat from the start.
- Decode the x-axis once before reading any figure. Ticks alternate F and S under academic-year labels; the omitted baseline is Spring 2019 (the invisible zero point under "18-19"), and the dashed line marks March 2020, not the baseline. Two exceptions matter: in Figure 3 the axis is annual with 2018-19 as baseline, and in panels 3c and 3d each point is the summer following the labeled academic year, so the point at "19-20" is summer 2020. Also remember the text's own caveat that attempted credits (1a, 2a) and persistence (3a, 3b) could not have been affected until Fall 2020, so the first point or two right of the dashed line in those panels are effectively still pre-period.
- You cannot judge effect sizes from the main text alone - get the Online Appendix if magnitudes matter to you. Table B1 holds baseline levels for every outcome; without it, a -0.5 credit or -0.05 share coefficient has no denominator. Figures B1 and B2 carry the full-time/part-time decomposition that is the substantive difference between the 4-year and 2-year attempted-credit stories, Figure B4 carries the developmental-education series needed to judge whether the 2-year pre-2020 trend is an artifact of the RISE reform, and Figures B5 through B16 hold the subgroup results for the five outcomes other than successful completion. Several main-text claims - that community-college subgroup gaps were driven by withdrawals while 4-year gaps were driven by D/F grades, and that a pre-pandemic gap-narrowing trend for URE and economically disadvantaged community college students was halted - rest entirely on appendix exhibits.
- Skim the Background section (roughly two and a half pages) unless you need the literature map; it is a broad survey of K-12 learning loss, online instruction, and grading policy that is not tied to specific empirical predictions. Do read the two paragraphs on North Carolina's grading-policy changes (the NCCCS WE/IE codes and the UNC System pass/satisfactory conversions) and footnote 4, which reports that pass-type grades jumped from about 1.5% to over 11% of 4-year courses in Spring 2020 - that footnote is what makes the Spring 2020 spikes interpretable and is easy to miss.
- Do not read the "female" finding as an established result. It appears in the abstract's headline list, gets one clause in Results and one in the Conclusion, and is never interpreted, despite the paper's own Background citing evidence that males have lower persistence and Table 1 showing the female share rising significantly in the 2020 and 2021 4-year cohorts. Figure 4d does show a real and reasonably precise relative gap of roughly 2 to 4 percentage points in the last two cohorts, but the paper gives a reader nothing to distinguish a behavioral change from a compositional one.
- Treat the summer-enrollment result as descriptive co-movement, not credit recovery. The Introduction's framing ("used the summer semesters to recover credits they failed to earn") is not tested - Outcomes says so explicitly, and footnote 5 reports that summer credits attempted and earned were flat conditional on enrolling. The timing also cuts against it: the largest summer increase follows 2019-20, the year 4-year credit earning rose.
- If a number is going into your own writing, re-derive it from the figure rather than taking the sentence. The verifiable ones are solid (0.75 credits, 5 pp, 11 pp, 9 pp, 1-2 pp), but "about 0.25 credits per semester" describes only the largest two of eight post-onset attempted-credit estimates, and "around 5 percentage points" for summer enrollment matches the last two years (approximately 0.049, 0.048) while understating the first two (approximately 0.067, 0.062).

**Detailed Commentary:**

One point of clarification about the published artifact: there is no intro-before-title layout problem in the published article. Page 1 of the PDF is cleanly typeset - Feature Article rubric, AERA masthead, title, byline with ORCID marks, abstract, keywords, submission dates, then the two-column Introduction. Any apparent inversion is an artifact of linear text extraction pulling the running-head and copyright block ahead of the title block. Equation typesetting is likewise fine in the PDF: Equation 1 renders as y_ijst = alpha_t + X_i'gamma + delta_j + eta_s + epsilon_ijst and Equation 2 renders its beta superscripts correctly; both are garbled only in extraction. Neither is a reader-facing problem.
