What is a reader-facing problem is the gap between the two registers the paper writes in. Inside the Results section, next to the figures, the prose is disciplined, hedged, and numerically accurate. Outside it - in the abstract, the Introduction's summary paragraph, and to a lesser degree the Conclusion - the same findings are restated in level language that the exhibits cannot bear. The clearest instance is the subgroup claim. Figure 4 reports beta-1 from Equation 2, the difference in deviations between a subgroup and its reference group. The paper explains this correctly twice, once in the Analyses section and once in the paragraph immediately before Figure 4, where it goes out of its way to warn that a negative coefficient "does not necessarily mean that the outcome decreased for the given subgroup." Yet the abstract says declines "have persisted for certain groups," and the Introduction says success rates "have not recovered to their baseline levels" for those groups. Baseline levels for subgroups are exactly what Figure 4 does not show, and beta-0 is not reported anywhere in the main text. A reader who stops at the abstract - which is most readers of an ER feature - will carry away a claim about levels that the article never demonstrates.

The internal-consistency question (Introduction says "not recovered," Results says "rebounded," Conclusion says "appear to be rebounding") turns out to be less serious than it looks, because these statements are about different populations: overall versus subgroups. The paper signposts the transition explicitly ("Later in this section, we show evidence that this is not the case for all students"). The real inconsistency is narrower and sits inside the 2-year discussion, where the text asserts a decrease "persisting for the later cohorts" and a "sustained increase in course withdrawals" while Figure 2c's final point is approximately +0.011 and Figure 2d's is approximately +0.007. The 2-year series is also visibly sawtoothed - fall semesters consistently worse than spring - which is surprising given that the figure notes say the dependent variables are already adjusted for prepandemic fall/spring differences, and which means the choice of endpoint drives the characterization. Neither the sawtooth nor the endpoint sensitivity is discussed.

The "starting in the fall of 2021" claim in the Introduction does check out for 4-year institutions: Figure 1c's first negative post-onset point is Fall 2021 at approximately -0.030, and Figure 1b drops from -0.08 in Spring 2021 to -0.58 in Fall 2021. Because the sentence follows a sentence about 4-year institutions and is followed by a sentence explicitly contrasting 2-year institutions ("as early as the Spring 2020 semester at 2-year institutions"), the sector-specificity is recoverable, though the sentence itself carries no sector qualifier.

On structure and density: for a 14-page format the organization is efficient and conventional, and a time-constrained reader can go straight to Results. The cost of that efficiency is that the article is a pointer to its appendix rather than a standalone document. Five exhibits appear in print; roughly eighteen appear online, including the only source of baseline levels, the only decomposition explaining why attempted credits fell differently in the two sectors, and subgroup results for five of six outcomes. Two substantive claims in the Results have no main-text exhibit at all - that community-college subgroup gaps were driven by withdrawals while 4-year gaps were driven by D/F grades, and that a pre-pandemic narrowing of gaps for URE and economically disadvantaged community college students was halted. The second of these is arguably the paper's most consequential inequality finding and it is a single sentence citing an appendix.

Table 1 deserves a specific note. It reports the 2018 baseline and the four pandemic cohorts but omits 2015 through 2017, even though those cohorts appear in every figure and are exactly the ones a reader would want in order to assess the "continuation of the preexisting trend" argument for attempted credits. The significance stars all test against 2018 only. The table is honest about composition change - it flags the rising Hispanic, ELL, and disability shares that predate the pandemic, and the AP/IB reweighting that mechanically depresses weighted GPA after 2018 - but it cannot answer the question the figures raise.

Confidence is limited in one respect: the full main text and all five main-text exhibits were examined at high resolution, but the Online Appendix, where much of the load-bearing evidence lives, was not available. Judgments about text-appendix fidelity are therefore inferences from how the main text describes the appendix, not verified readings of it. Figure coefficient values reported here are read off the plots to roughly the nearest half-hundredth and should be treated as approximations, though the comparisons they support - which points are above or below zero, which confidence intervals cross it, and relative magnitudes across panels - are not close calls.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This paper documents descriptive trends in first-year college credit earning, completion, withdrawal, persistence, and summer enrollment for eight North Carolina high school cohorts (2015-2022) using linked NCDPI-UNC System-NCCCS administrative records covering roughly 403,000 immediate enrollees across 16 public universities and 58 community colleges. Its genuine additions are the scope of the linked statewide data across both sectors and a time horizon that reaches the high school class of 2022 (first year in 2022-23), well past the Spring-2020 window that dominates the existing US postsecondary COVID literature, plus subgroup-specific recovery gaps at that scale. Much of the aggregate story, however, confirms rather than extends prior work, and the headline claim about persistent declines rests on relative subgroup contrasts in a policy-sensitive outcome, not on absolute levels.

**Strengths:**

- The data asset is genuinely rare and hard to replicate: statewide K-12 records linked to transcript-level course data from both the entire public 4-year system and all 58 community colleges, for eight cohorts. Few states can support this, and it lets the paper speak to institutional and student heterogeneity that single-institution studies (Rodriguez-Planas 2022a, 2022b; Kuperman et al. 2026) and single-sector studies (Bird et al. 2022; Bulman & Fairlie 2022) cannot.
- The time horizon is the paper's clearest contribution. Almost all existing US evidence on postsecondary performance stops at Spring 2020 or Fall 2021. Extending through the 2022-23 academic year lets the paper make a point no prior study could: the largest 4-year declines occur in 2021-22, not Spring 2020, i.e., after the acute disruption, plausibly reflecting the arrival of pandemic-affected high school cohorts rather than contemporaneous college disruption.
- Sector contrast is informative and well-drawn. The mechanism differs by sector in a way that is visible and policy-relevant: at 4-year institutions declines run through D/F grades with withdrawals essentially flat (Figure 1d), while at community colleges they run through a sustained withdrawal/incomplete increase that spikes 11 percentage points in Spring 2020 and stays elevated through 2022 (Figure 2d).
- The summer-enrollment result (Figure 3c: roughly a 5 percentage point increase in 4-year summer coursetaking starting 2020, with no corresponding early increase at 2-year institutions) is a novel and underexplored margin, and yields a concrete, actionable policy point about summer capacity as a recovery channel.
- The paper is honest about its descriptive status in the Conclusion, explicitly naming concurrent confounds (economic shocks, stimulus, 2020 political unrest) and declining to claim causal identification. It also flags composition change as a threat and adjusts for observables, high school fixed effects, and institution fixed effects.
- An underexploited robustness point works in the paper's favor: at 2-year institutions the shares of economically disadvantaged and below-median-GPA students fell for the 2021 and 2022 cohorts (Table 1, Panel B), so the observable composition of the community college sample improved even as outcomes worsened, making simple negative selection an unlikely full explanation for the 2-year declines.

**Weaknesses:**

- The central outcome is not a learning measure. "Successful course completion" and "earned credits" are jointly produced by student performance and institutional grading rules, and those rules changed substantially and non-uniformly during the study window (UNC flexible pass/satisfactory conversion, NCCCS WE/IE emergency grades). The paper demonstrates this for Spring 2020 -- the +5pp completion jump at 4-year institutions and the 11pp withdrawal jump at 2-year institutions are essentially policy artifacts -- but then reads the 2021-22 movements in the same measure as substantive academic decline without documenting when and how completely those policies reverted.
- The abstract's most quotable claim outruns what the figures show. "These declines have persisted" is true of subgroup gaps, but the aggregate series in Figures 1c and 2c return to roughly baseline by Spring 2023. The paper's own text concedes 4-year credit earning "appears to have recovered." A reader who takes the abstract at face value will overstate the aggregate persistence.
- The female result -- the abstract's most novel and therefore most citable subgroup -- is the weakest of the four. In Figure 4d the estimates are roughly 2-3 percentage points, the smallest in the figure, and they are differences relative to male students. Because women historically outperform men on these outcomes, a negative coefficient is consistent with women's completion falling, men's rising, or both, and the paper never shows subgroup levels in the main text. The authors state this caveat in the Results section but not in the abstract, where the claim will actually be read and cited.
- The strongest subgroup finding rests on a measure the pandemic itself contaminated. "Below-median high school GPA" is a within-cohort relative rank, and NC high school grading during 2020-2022 was affected by grade inflation and emergency grading, and by two state GPA policy changes (7-point to 10-point scale in 2015-16; reduced AP/IB weighting effective with the class of 2019, visible as the sharp weighted-GPA drop after 2018 in Table 1). Below-median in the 2021 cohort plausibly identifies a differently-composed group than in the 2018 cohort.
- A large NC-specific confound is relegated to an appendix. The RISE developmental education reform ran 2019-2020 and was paused in 2021, moving community college students out of remedial coursework and into credit-bearing math and English. This maps almost exactly onto the 2-year decline window and onto the outcome that is measured, yet it appears only in a footnote-and-appendix treatment rather than as a modeled alternative explanation.
- Pre-trends are not uniformly clean, and the paper is inconsistent about them. At 4-year institutions attempted credits are declining before 2020 and the authors correctly read the post-2020 decline as trend continuation. At 2-year institutions the pre-period is visibly noisy (Figure 2a swings from about -0.45 to +0.15) and summer coursetaking is on a strong pre-existing upward trend (Figure 3d), which complicates baseline-deviation readings that are not similarly discounted.
- The analysis is thin relative to the data. Six event-study figures and one subgroup figure in the main text, with essentially everything else -- all non-completion subgroup results, developmental education, full-time/part-time, D/F shares, enrollment composition -- pushed to an unpublished-with-the-text online appendix. No institution-type heterogeneity within the UNC System (selectivity, HBCU status), no decomposition of composition versus performance, no attempt to bound the grading-policy contribution.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite it for: the best current US descriptive evidence that first-year postsecondary performance declines associated with the pandemic were largest for cohorts arriving in 2021-22, not for students enrolled during the acute Spring 2020 disruption. This timing point is the paper's most defensible novel claim and follows directly from Figures 1b, 1c, 2b, and 2c.
- Cite it for: the sector contrast in mechanism -- 4-year declines driven by D/F grades with flat withdrawals, 2-year declines driven by a sustained withdrawal and incomplete increase. This is cleanly shown, large, and consistent across specifications.
- Cite it for: replication and extension of Bulman & Fairlie (2022) on the Spring 2020 community college withdrawal spike, and of Rodriguez-Planas (2022a) on flexible grading disproportionately helping lower-performing students -- now shown in a second state, across an entire public system, and with a multi-year follow-on window neither study had.
- Cite it for: the summer-term recovery margin at 4-year institutions, but as suggestive only -- the authors explicitly do not test whether summer enrollment is in courses the student previously withdrew from or failed.
- Do not lean on it for: the claim that college outcomes have not recovered overall. The aggregate completion series return to roughly baseline by Spring 2023; only relative subgroup gaps persist.
- Do not lean on it for: the claim that female college students are now performing worse than male students. The coefficients are male-referenced differences in change, not levels, and the paper shows no subgroup level comparison in the main text.
- Do not lean on it for: causal statements about pandemic effects. The paper has no untreated comparison group -- all cohorts were exposed -- and the authors say so directly; concurrent grading reforms, RISE, stimulus payments, and labor market shocks are not separated.
- Do not lean on it for: generalization beyond first-year, immediately enrolling, in-state public NC students. It excludes gap-year and delayed enrollees, out-of-state and private institutions, and everything past the first year -- exclusions that matter most at community colleges, where older and non-immediate students are a large share of enrollment.
- Do not lean on it for: statements about learning loss carrying into college. The outcomes are institutional credit and grade records that grading policy directly manipulates, not assessments.
- Open questions a reader should know remain: whether these first-year gaps translate into degree completion or later-year persistence (deferred to Eilam et al. 2026); whether the 4-year rebound holds for cohorts after 2022; whether declines reflect academic preparation, engagement, non-academic constraints, or institutional response; whether grading policies had fully reverted by 2021-22; and whether the pattern replicates in states without NC's specific developmental education and GPA policy changes.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Where this stands in the literature. On its narrow question -- how first-year performance at public 2- and 4-year institutions evolved for cohorts entering before, during, and after the pandemic -- this is plausibly now the best available US evidence, for two reasons that are about data rather than method. First, the horizon: Bird et al. (2022), Bulman & Fairlie (2022), and Rodriguez-Planas (2022a) all stop at or near Spring 2020; Howell et al. (2022) reaches Fall 2021; Westrick et al. (2024) covers the classes of 2020-2021. Reaching the high school class of 2022 lets this paper make an observation the earlier literature structurally could not, namely that the deepest declines arrive after the acute disruption, when high school cohorts whose own secondary education was disrupted begin entering college. Second, the coverage: an entire state's public system in both sectors, linked to K-12 records, with roughly 403,000 students. Against that, the analytical contribution is modest. The method is a conditional event study with cohort and semester indicators; the aggregate results largely confirm findings already in the literature; and the paper leaves most of its data unexploited in the main text.

The quotable-versus-supported gap. The abstract's list -- "underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, economically disadvantaged and academically weaker students, as well as female students" -- reads as four findings of comparable standing. Figure 4 does not support that reading. The below-median-HS-GPA result at 4-year institutions is large and unambiguous (roughly -0.09 in Fall 2021, still around -0.06 at the end of the sample) and is the paper's strongest subgroup finding. The URE and economically disadvantaged results are modest, in the 2-4 percentage point range, with the 2-year estimates generally larger than the 4-year ones. The female result is the smallest. Yet the female finding is the most surprising and therefore the most likely to be lifted into secondary citation, where the male-reference-group framing will not survive the trip. Readers relying on this paper should treat the academic-preparation gradient as the headline and the gender contrast as a flag for further work.

On framing honesty. The paper is better than average here but not fully consistent. The title's "Gaps in Recovery From the COVID-19 Pandemic" is defensible as descriptive language, the abstract says "during and after" rather than "caused by," and the Conclusion contains an unusually direct disclaimer that the study cannot disentangle the pandemic from concurrent events. But causal phrasing leaks back in elsewhere -- "post-COVID-19 changes," "the pandemic appears to have ended this trend" -- and the Sample section's important restrictions (immediate enrollees only, first year only, public in-state only) never surface in the abstract. The boundary-drawing is honest where a careful reader will find it, and invisible where a casual citer will not.

A structural caution about the sample. Conditioning on immediate enrollment at an NC public institution selects on a margin the pandemic moved. Footnote 3 concedes as much: 2-year enrollment fell overall, with the largest drops among low-achievement, economically disadvantaged, and English-learner students, while top-quartile-GPA graduates shifted toward 2-year institutions. Covariate adjustment addresses the observable part of this. It does not address the possibility that the students who continued to enroll differ on unobserved dimensions from those who did not, and the direction of that bias differs by sector -- likely attenuating the 2-year declines and potentially inflating them at 4-year institutions if stronger students left the sector. This is genuinely hard to fix in a descriptive design and is not a fatal flaw, but it should temper any use of the subgroup magnitudes as point estimates rather than as directional evidence.

What the paper sets up. It functions in part as the flagship descriptive entry in a three-paper NC Collaboratory project, with enrollment and multi-year persistence in Eilam et al. (2026) and qualitative staff and student perceptions in Hutchins et al. (2026). The advising finding it borrows from the qualitative companion -- that advisors steered underprepared community college students toward lighter loads -- is the most interesting causal hypothesis in the paper and is entirely untested here. That is a reasonable division of labor, but it means the reader cannot yet evaluate the paper's most policy-relevant mechanism claim on the evidence presented.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The article documents its sample construction and variable definitions unusually carefully for a short-format Educational Researcher feature — data sources, exclusions, grade-to-outcome mappings, and the two estimating equations are all spelled out in prose — but it contains no data availability statement, no documented access pathway for the restricted linked NCDPI–UNC System–NCCCS records, no replication code or stated software environment, and no numeric results whatsoever: every headline finding is a coefficient plot, so not one quantity quoted in the text can be checked against a reported number. Understanding the study is easy; verifying it from what is published is effectively impossible, and a would-be replicator with data access would still have to guess at the outcome transformation that underlies every main figure.

**Strengths:**

- Data sources are named precisely and at the right level of granularity: course-level UNC System and NCCCS transcript records (attempted credits, earned credits, quality points, final letter grade including withdrawal grades) linked by unique student identifier to NCDPI K-12 records supplying graduation year, graduating school, weighted cumulative GPA, demographics, NCDPI-determined economically disadvantaged status, EL status, and disability status. A reader knows exactly what universe of records the study rests on, and the funding note names the underlying IES data set by grant number (R305H190036, UNC Greensboro) — a concrete hook a replicator could pursue even though the paper itself does not describe an access route.
- Sample restrictions are stated with enough specificity to be largely rebuildable: fall and spring semesters following the high school graduation date only (excluding summer bridge, gap-year entrants, dual-credit courses earned in high school, out-of-system enrollment, and anything past year one); exclusion of courses with zero or missing attempted credits, developmental education courses, and courses whose grading scale is "audit," "transfer," or "not graded"; and exclusion of students who did not attend an NC public high school (mechanically imposed by the NCDPI link). The persistence sample's additional exclusion of spring-entering students is quantified (3% of the UNC sample, 14% of NCCCS), which is more than most papers report.
- Outcome definitions are given at the grade-code level rather than in the abstract: credit earned means C (2.0) or better plus "Satisfactory," "Pass," and "High Pass"; non-completion means W, I/IN, or IP; the residual D/F category is explicitly named as the complement. Footnote 4 goes further and reports the base rate of S/P/HP grades (about 1.5% of 4-year courses, rising above 11% in Spring 2020) and notes that "Pass" in the community college data attaches almost exclusively to developmental or non-credit courses that are dropped — exactly the kind of institutional detail that determines whether a replication's numbers match.
- Known threats to variable comparability across years are disclosed rather than buried: footnote 2 documents North Carolina's 7-point to 10-point grading scale switch (2015–2016) and the reduction of the AP/IB GPA bonus from two points to one (class of 2019), and explains the resulting harmonization choice — using within-cohort relative GPA rank. The corresponding level shift is visible in Table 1 (weighted HS GPA falls from 4.130 in 2018 to 3.775 in 2019 at 4-year institutions), so the reader can see the problem and the authors' response to it in the same paper.
- The estimating equations are printed, and the figure notes independently restate the specification: covariates (gender, race/ethnicity categories, economically disadvantaged, EL, disability, below-median HS GPA), high school and postsecondary institution fixed effects, Spring 2019 as the omitted semester (2018–19 as the omitted academic year), 95% confidence intervals, and standard errors clustered by postsecondary institution. Equation 2's interpretation — that the plotted coefficients are differences-in-deviations relative to the complementary reference group, not subgroup-specific changes — is stated in the text and repeated in the Figure 4 note, which forecloses the single most common misreading of that exhibit.
- Internal consistency of the reported sample counts holds up under a simple check: Table 1's five reported cohorts sum to 133,154 students at 4-year institutions and 121,226 at 2-year institutions, leaving roughly 76,900 and 71,600 for the three unreported 2015–2017 cohorts — average cohort sizes of about 25,600 and 23,900, closely in line with the reported cohorts. The headline sample sizes of 210,008 and 192,793 are therefore at least arithmetically coherent.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement. The entire supplementary apparatus is the boilerplate line "Supplemental material is available online," which points to an Online Appendix of additional exhibits, not to data or code. The article never states who holds the linked file, under what agreement it was assembled, whether it sits with the UNC Greensboro IES-funded project, the NC Collaboratory, an NCDPI/UNC System/NCCCS data-sharing arrangement, or a state longitudinal data system, and never describes how another researcher would apply for equivalent access. Restricted data cannot be posted, and no reviewer should expect it to be — but the pathway can always be documented, and here it is not documented at all. A replicator's first question ("whom do I write to?") has no answer in the article.
- No replication package, no posted code, not even "code available upon request." The software environment is never named — no package, no version, no estimation command. The estimator itself is never stated: Equations 1 and 2 are written as linear indexes and the outcomes include three binary variables (fall-to-spring persistence, summer enrollment, and implicitly the share measures bounded in [0,1]), so the reader must infer OLS/linear probability throughout. Nothing is said about weighting (presumably none), about how observations with missing covariates are handled (listwise deletion is the natural guess but is never stated), or about how a student enrolled at two institutions in the same term is assigned to the single institution fixed effect δ_j.
- The transformation applied to every dependent variable in the main figures is described in one sentence and then deferred. The figure notes to Figures 1, 2, and 4 all say "The dependent variables are adjusted for underlying prepandemic differences between the fall and spring semesters," and the Analyses section illustrates the intent with the community-college fall/spring credit example, but the actual procedure — is it a pre-2020 fall indicator residualized out, a semester-specific demeaning estimated on 2015–2019 data, a two-step where residuals from a first-stage regression become the outcome, and if so how the second-stage standard errors account for the first stage — is never given, only pointed to as "more details ... in Online Appendix A." This is not a robustness check; it is the construction of the plotted outcome, and as reported in the main text it cannot be reproduced. Every quantity in Figures 1, 2, and 4 is downstream of a step the article does not specify.
- No results are reported numerically. There are no coefficient tables anywhere in the article — Figures 1 through 4 are the entire results section, and they carry no printed point estimates, no standard errors, no p-values, and no per-panel sample sizes. Consequently the specific magnitudes the text asserts ("about 0.25 credits per semester," "a pronounced jump of around 0.75 hours," "an increase of around 5 percentage points in successful course completion," the "11 percentage point" rise and "9 percentage point" fall at community colleges in Spring 2020, the "1 to 2 percentage point" persistence decline against a 95% baseline) can only be eyeballed against plotted markers. A reader cannot confirm any of them, cannot recover the standard errors, and cannot use any of these estimates in a meta-analysis or a power calculation for follow-on work.
- Sample sizes are reported inconsistently and at the wrong unit. Figures 1 and 2 report unique student counts (210,008 and 192,793); Figures 3 and 4 report no N at all. Because each student contributes their first fall and first spring, the semester-frequency regressions are estimated on student-semester observations whose count is never given, and the persistence and summer-enrollment regressions run on yet another, smaller sample after the 3% / 14% spring-starter exclusion — a number the article never states in levels. The number of clusters is also never reported, which matters directly: clustering at the institution level yields roughly 16 clusters in the UNC sample, well into the range where a cluster-robust variance estimator is known to under-cover, and the article offers no small-cluster correction, no wild bootstrap, and no acknowledgment of the issue.
- Several construction details a replication would immediately trip over are left implicit. "Immediate enrollment" is defined only as observations in the fall and spring following the graduation date, with no statement of how a graduation date is assigned for off-cycle or summer completers. The persistence rule requires re-enrollment "at any public in-state institution of the same level," which mechanically codes a 4-year-to-community-college move as non-persistence but never says so. The below-median HS GPA indicator is used both as a covariate and as the subgroup split, while footnote 2 says the analyses "focus on a student's relative GPA rank within their cohort" — two different constructs, and the article never resolves which enters Equation 1, nor over what population the median is drawn (Table 1's 0.179 at 4-year versus 0.624 at 2-year implies a statewide rather than sector-specific median, but the reader has to reverse-engineer that). Footnote 1 discloses that part-of-term courses are not differentiated in the data and that the two 4-year summer terms are aggregated, which is honest, but no rule is given for how a part-of-term course is assigned to fall or spring.
- The exclusion documentation is not applied consistently across exhibits. The Figure 2 note states "Developmental education courses are excluded from the analyses"; the Figure 1 note does not, even though the Data section applies the exclusion globally and 4-year institutions also offer developmental coursework. Similarly, "Each set of coefficient estimates comes from a separate regression" appears only in the Figure 2 note (preceded by a stray "(a)" that reads as a typesetting artifact), though it must hold for Figures 1, 3, and 4 as well. Small discrepancies like these are exactly where a replication diverges.
- Table 1 covers only five of the eight cohorts. The 2015, 2016, and 2017 cohorts — roughly 148,000 students, and the cohorts that do most of the work of establishing the prepandemic trend against which every postpandemic deviation is judged — have no reported descriptive statistics anywhere in the main text, so a reader cannot assess composition drift over the very period the pre-trend is drawn from. Baseline descriptives for the outcomes themselves are also absent from the article, deferred to Online Appendix Table B1, which means even the level of, say, the successful-completion rate that a 5-percentage-point change is measured against is unavailable in the published article.
- No human-subjects, IRB, or data-use-agreement statement appears, and no disclosure of any disclosure-avoidance rules (cell-size suppression, rounding) that a state administrative data agreement typically imposes — relevant both to whether the reported subgroup analyses were constrained and to what a future data recipient could publish.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat every numeric magnitude in the Results and Conclusion as unverified. None of them is printed in a table, and the figures show markers without values, so a reader who wants to cite "0.25 credits," "around 5 percentage points," or "a 1 to 2 percentage point decrease in persistence" should either read them off the plots as approximations with visible uncertainty or write to the corresponding author (Dora Gicheva, d_gichev@uncg.edu) for the underlying coefficient tables. Do not carry these point estimates into a meta-analysis, a benchmark, or a power calculation without obtaining the standard errors, which are nowhere reported.
- Before relying on any main figure, request Online Appendix A and read what the fall/spring adjustment actually is. Every plotted coefficient in Figures 1, 2, and 4 is estimated on an adjusted dependent variable whose construction the main text does not specify. Specifically ask whether the adjustment is estimated on prepandemic data only, whether it is a residualization performed in a first stage, and whether the reported standard errors and 95% CIs account for that first stage. If the answer is that residuals from a first-stage regression are used as outcomes without correction, the intervals in the main figures are understated by an unknown amount, and the borderline results (the Spring 2020 fall-to-spring persistence estimates, the Fall 2022 rebound estimates) are the ones most affected.
- Check the sample sizes yourself before comparing across exhibits. Figures 1 and 2 report unique students (210,008 and 192,793) while Figures 3 and 4 report none, and the persistence analyses drop 3% of the 4-year and 14% of the 2-year sample. That 14% is a large, non-random exclusion at community colleges — spring entrants are plausibly the least attached students — so the 2-year persistence trends in Figure 3b describe a materially different population than the credit-earning trends in Figure 2. Do not read the two panels as describing the same students.
- Be skeptical of the confidence intervals in the 4-year figures specifically. Standard errors are clustered by postsecondary institution and the UNC System contains 16 four-year institutions; the number of clusters is never reported and no small-cluster correction is mentioned. With roughly that many clusters, conventional cluster-robust intervals under-cover, so the 95% bands in Figures 1, 3a, 3c, and the four-year series in Figure 4 should be read as optimistic. The 58-institution community college estimates are on safer ground.
- If you intend to replicate, budget for a data-access negotiation the article does not describe. Start from the IES grant named in the funding statement (R305H190036, University of North Carolina at Greensboro) and the NC Collaboratory award (SLFRP0129), and expect to approach NCDPI, the UNC System Office, and the NC Community College System separately, since nothing in the article documents a single custodian or a standing application route. Ask the authors directly whether the linked analysis file can be made available to a subsequent researcher under the existing agreements or whether the link must be rebuilt from scratch.
- If you obtain the data, expect to make at least these judgment calls without guidance from the paper, and pre-register them: whether the estimator is OLS/LPM for the binary persistence and summer outcomes; how observations with missing covariates are handled; how a student enrolled at two institutions in one term is assigned to the institution fixed effect; how part-of-term courses (which footnote 1 says are undifferentiated in the data) map to fall versus spring; whether the below-median GPA split and the within-cohort GPA rank are the same variable or two, and over which population the median is computed; and whether the developmental-education exclusion is applied at 4-year institutions as the Figure 1 note's silence leaves ambiguous. Each of these can move the estimates, and none is resolvable from the article.
- Ask for the descriptives the article omits before judging the pre-trend. Table 1 shows only the 2018–2022 cohorts, but the prepandemic baseline against which everything is measured rests on the 2015–2017 cohorts, whose composition is never reported in the main text. Request their characteristics along with Online Appendix Table B1 (baseline outcome levels for Fall 2018 / Spring 2019) — without the latter, the reported percentage-point changes have no denominator a reader can see.
- The findings that are most robust to these transparency gaps are the large, directionally unambiguous ones: the Spring 2020 spike in successful completion at 4-year institutions alongside flat withdrawals (a pattern corroborated by the disclosed policy change and by Rodríguez-Planas, 2022a), and the sustained Spring-2020-onward rise in community college withdrawals (corroborated independently by Bulman & Fairlie, 2022, in California). The findings most dependent on unverifiable machinery are the subgroup differences-in-deviations in Figure 4, where the estimates are small, the CIs frequently span zero, the reference-group interpretation is subtle, and the adjusted outcome is the unspecified one — lean on the qualitative pattern there, not on any individual coefficient.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Scope note: the Online Appendix was not available for this assessment, so it covers only what the published article documents. That distinction matters here more than usual, because the appendix is load-bearing. Online Appendix A is where the empirical approach is elaborated, Online Appendix B holds the baseline outcome descriptives (Table B1), the enrollment-shift evidence (Table B2), the full-time/part-time decompositions (Figures B1, B2), the developmental education trends (Figure B4), the D/F results, and all subgroup analyses for the five outcomes other than successful completion (Figures B5–B16). A reader who does not download the supplement is seeing a substantially thinner paper than the authors wrote. What the appendix cannot supply, however, is a data availability statement, an access pathway, code, or coefficient tables — the article gives no indication that any of those exist.

Where the paper is genuinely strong is the descriptive documentation of construction. The Data Source, Sample, and Outcomes subsections do real work: they name the source systems, the linking key, the excluded course types, the excluded student types, the grade codes that map to each outcome, the base rates of the unusual grade codes, and the two North Carolina GPA policy changes that break comparability across cohorts along with the harmonization response. Footnotes 1 through 6 carry more methodological content than the notes in most articles of this length, including candid disclosures of data limitations (part-of-term courses undifferentiated; summer terms aggregated) and of analyses run but not shown. Someone reading to understand what was done will not be confused. That is a real accomplishment in a 14-page format and it is why this review does not land at "insufficient."

Where it fails is verification, and the failure is layered. The outermost layer is access: there is no statement of who holds the linked file or how to request it. Restricted administrative data legitimately cannot be posted, and the absence of a public dataset is not itself a shortcoming — but the absence of any documented route to the data is, and it is entirely within the authors' control to fix in two sentences. The IES grant number and the NC Collaboratory award number in the funding statement are the only handles a replicator has, and they are there by publisher convention rather than by design.

The next layer is code and specification. No package is deposited, none is promised, no software is named, and the estimator is left to inference. More consequentially, the one non-obvious data transformation in the whole paper — the adjustment of each dependent variable for prepandemic fall/spring differences — is asserted in the figure notes and explained by analogy in the text ("community college students tend to attempt slightly more credits in the fall") but never operationalized. Because this adjustment is applied to the outcome, not to the covariates, it sits upstream of every coefficient in Figures 1, 2, and 4. If it is a residualization performed in a separate first-stage regression, the plotted 95% intervals are conditional on estimated quantities and are too narrow by an unquantified amount. The article gives the reader no way to know which situation obtains. That single deferral does more damage to verifiability than all the smaller ambiguities combined.

The outermost failure is reporting. There is not one table of results in this article. Six outcomes, two sectors, four subgroup splits, sixteen semester coefficients per series — and the entire evidentiary base is four coefficient plots. The plots are competently made (uniform axes within panels, visible 95% CIs, a clear pandemic-onset reference line, consistent semester labeling), and the figure notes are unusually complete about the specification. But no number in the Results section can be checked. When the text says withdrawals and incompletes "increased by 11 percentage points in the spring of 2020," the reader can confirm only that the corresponding marker in Figure 2d sits somewhere near 0.11 with a CI running roughly 0.06 to 0.16. Precision, significance at the margin, and any use of these estimates as inputs to other work are all foreclosed.

A related and easily missed problem is that sample sizes are reported at a unit that does not match the estimation. Figures 1 and 2 give unique student counts; the regressions are run on student-semester observations, since each student contributes a fall and a spring. Figures 3 and 4 give no N at all, and the persistence sample has been reduced by 3% and 14% respectively without the resulting counts appearing anywhere. The number of clusters — the quantity that actually determines whether the reported inference is trustworthy — is never stated, and with the UNC System containing 16 four-year institutions, it is small enough that it should have been.

Taken together: the paper is well documented as a description and poorly documented as a verifiable empirical claim. A knowledgeable reader can reconstruct what the authors intended to do; a replicator with the data in hand would still face a half-dozen consequential unspecified choices, and a reader without the data has no numeric quantity to check against anything. "Weak" is the right rating, though it sits close to the "adequate" boundary on the strength of the sample and variable documentation. The two changes that would move it most are also the cheapest: a data availability statement naming a custodian and an application route, and an appendix table of the plotted coefficients with their standard errors.
